entries.title: Array sort with a comparator
entries.body: `xs.sort(cmp)` sorts in place, stably, and answers the array, element for element in Node's order for any consistent comparator. The sort is `std/sort.ts`'s `sortWith`, a bottom-up merge sort over runs of 32 sorted by insertion, with one scratch allocation. It is instantiated once per comparator and calls the comparator directly. A comparator may read the caller's `const` locals and parameters. `xs.sort()` with no comparator (NL2620), a second argument (NL2619), a readonly array and `process.argv` are refused.
metrics: 100,000 elements x 20, median of 5 at --profile speed; 1.6x (i32 reversed) to 9.9x (f64 random) faster than Node's Array.prototype.sort, level with or ahead of a hand-written Nish merge sort except i32 random/ties (+3%/+8%, within noise)

entries.title: fetch apt packages from mirrors other than Azure's, and cache every install
entries.body:
* ci: fetch apt packages from mirrors other than Azure's, and cache every install

Every Ubuntu install in CI now goes through .github/actions/apt-install,
which first runs .github/apt-mirror.sh. The script points every apt
source that names the Azure host or the main Ubuntu archive at a mirror
list of our own: mirrors.edge.kernel.org, then archive.ubuntu.com, then
security.ubuntu.com. apt moves down that list when a mirror fails.

The inline rewrite it replaces piped `grep -rlZ azure... | xargs sed`
under `pipefail`. On a runner image that names no Azure host, grep exits
1 and the install step failed in about 70 ms, before apt printed a line.
That failed the v0.31.0 release's bootstrap job and #1158's fuzz-smoke.

The installs that were still inline now use the cached action: the
`test` shards, interop's tshark, ct-timing, rebuild and the release
binaries. Homebrew installs go through a new
.github/actions/brew-install, which keeps the bottles in the Actions
cache. The pinned h2spec tarball is cached by its SHA-256. A restored
.deb, bottle or tarball is still checked against its hash before it is
used.

Refs: docs/wp10-ci.md
Tests: actionlint, shellcheck, apt-mirror.sh run against a real apt

* test(cli): check the watch server swap loses nothing only where Linux can promise it

When `nish run --watch` swaps a server, the old one closes its
SO_REUSEPORT listener while the new one is up. Linux resets every
connection still queued on a closing listener unless
net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req is 1 (Linux 5.14+), in which case the kernel
moves them to another listener in the group. So a connection queued
between the old server's last accept and its close was reset whatever
the server did, and the check that no request is lost across the swap
failed at random (#1158's shard 1, ECONNRESET).

CI's `test` job now turns the setting on. Without it the check is a
counted skip that names the setting, instead of a coin toss. The CLI
guide no longer says that SO_REUSEPORT plus draining on SIGTERM is
enough on Linux. It now names the setting as well.

Tests: node tests/run.js watch (26 passed, three runs, with the setting; 25 passed and 1 skipped without it)

entries.title: bcrypt batch kernels take two index bytes from one copy
entries.body:
bcryptBody3 to bcryptBody6 now write each lane's half-round whole before the
next lane's, and take the two middle S-box index bytes from one copy of the
word moved down by 8 behind the value barrier (`ctSelect(v, ~0, 0)`), so LLVM
copies the word once instead of twice and spills less. Three to five lanes
rotate the copy, which a BMI2 build lowers to one `rorx`; six shift it.
bcryptBody2 and the single path are unchanged. Every hash is byte for byte
the same.

bench/crypto/bcrypt/kernel/gen-tight.mjs adds two hand kernels to
ceiling.mjs, after the extraction styles of the multicore-server-challenge's
leading entries: `shrx` (zig-iouring-nick-potts, also rust-epoll-theCatWisel)
and `dh` (asm-epoll-nickita-khylkouski). The record's new "Cascade Lake"
section has the ceiling on a Xeon Platinum 8260, 15% at the old best width
and 7 to 9% now, under the 20% bar for a runtime kernel.
metrics: Xeon Platinum 8260, cost 10, five lanes (the best width): 22.7 (22.4-23.5) -> 21.3 (21.0-21.8) ms a hash, -6.5%, and -5.8% in a second pass; --cpu x86-64-v3 22.2 -> 20.7 ms, -6.7%; 15 interleaved rounds, spreads about 2%
